Munters (MTRS-SE): a pre-sold 2027 earnings step at a trough multiple that already prices a 20% cut to consensus; the risk lies in one plant's margin, not in demand

Written 7 November 2026, four days before Munters' Capital Markets Day (CMD) on 11 November 2026. Share price SEK 131.45 (25 October 2026). Forecasts are Viewforth's (adjusted EPS SEK 7.60 for 2027 and SEK 9.51 for 2028); consensus is the FactSet median. Money is in SEK millions unless stated. Sources, conventions and a glossary are in the end notes.

0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in brief. Munters has pre-sold its next two years of revenue, so the investment case turns on one plant's margin rather than on demand.

Demand is secure. A backlog of SEK 28bn (1.8x sales, up 178% year on year), built on cooling for AI data centres, makes 2027 revenue of about SEK 20bn (+20%) close to certain. Most of the 2027 earnings step is mechanical: more volume through a plant that is already built, tariff relief as US chiller production localises, an AirTech cost programme that is already delivered, and overheads that grew 2% in Q3 2026 while sales grew 18%.

One margin decides the share price. The element that is not mechanical is the margin that the Data Center Technologies (DCT) division earns on each unit shipped from its plant in Daleville, Virginia. DCT's adjusted EBITA margin fell to 9.7% in Q3 2026 from 19.5% a year earlier. Excluding tariffs, DCT's margin was still falling while its volume rose 32% quarter on quarter.

Consensus assumes a recovery Munters has never shown. The sell-side has written off 2026 and moved the lost earnings into 2027 without cutting them. Consensus 2027 EPS of SEK 9.77 (+95%) needs a DCT margin of 17% to 20% in the first full year after a troubled ramp, a recovery at Vertiv's speed. Our base case is SEK 7.60 for 2027 (DCT margin 14.7%, group adjusted EBITA margin 13.3%), 22% below consensus, and SEK 9.51 for 2028, 21% below.

The share price has already discounted roughly that cut. The shares fell 33% in six months while cooling peers rose 10%. On consensus EPS the two-year-forward P/E is 11.35x, the 2nd percentile of its five-year range; on our EPS it is about 14.2x, almost exactly the guideline fair multiple of 14.77x. Munters is therefore not a re-rating case. It is an earnings-delivery case, bought at a multiple that already assumes the sell-side is wrong by a fifth.

The share price has moved ahead of the estimate cuts, so the return must come from earnings delivery, not from a re-rating.

The seven insights that matter most

1

The share price has already moved ahead of the coming estimate cuts.

The market's implied view of Munters is harsher than the sell-side's, where 91% of brokers rate the shares a Buy and the median target is SEK 200. Cuts of 10% to 15% to 2027 consensus EPS are probable by April 2027, because four of the brokers who set the median have not updated since the Q3 report, and the two who have updated sit at SEK 8.0 to 8.8. On our numbers those cuts are largely in the price already. The risk over the next six months is therefore estimate cuts arriving into a share price that has already fallen: uncomfortable, but not the same as downside.

2

DCT's margin problem has moved from the tariff to the ramp.

US Section 232 tariffs cost DCT 2 points of margin in Q3 2026. Before tariffs, DCT's margin was about 11.7%, about 300 basis points lower than in Q2 despite far higher volume (calculated). Two causes now matter more than the tariff: inefficiency in the Daleville ramp, and prices in the old backlog meeting 2026 costs. Removing the tariff is a task to complete; ramping a plant efficiently is a capability Munters has not yet shown in this cycle. On 23 October the CEO described the tariff work as moving "from full localisation to optimisation", which makes a residual tariff cost through all of 2027 (about SEK 50m to 60m, or SEK 0.2 of EPS) a live risk.

3

Three-quarters of the 2027 profit step rests on demonstrated or mechanical ground.

In our model, group adjusted EBITA rises by SEK 779m from 2026 to 2027. Four parts of that rise rest on facts already observed or on arithmetic: volume at the 2026 margin (+SEK 373m), tariff removal (+115m), AirTech savings (+70m) and lower corporate costs (+20m). Two parts need execution: ramp efficiency (+120m) and net price over cost (+80m). The direction of the recovery is therefore well founded, but its timing is not. Recoveries of this kind take four to eight quarters from the trough, here Q3 or Q4 2026, and Munters' own recovery of 2017 to 2019 took two years. That base rate points to H2 2027, a quarter later than management implies.

4

Cash lags earnings, and consensus misses the lag.

Customer advances of SEK 4.1bn fund the ramp and hold operating working capital at 4.2% of sales. When 2027 orders (about SEK 22bn) fall below 2026 orders (about SEK 27.5bn), the advance float stops growing. Our 2027 free cash flow is therefore SEK 555m, against consensus of SEK 1,426m. Leverage still falls, from 3.4x to about 2.1x net debt to EBITDA by end-2027, because EBITDA grows. A sale of FoodTech would take leverage below 1x (net proceeds about SEK 4.3bn, or about SEK 24 a share, calculated).

5

The case is concentrated on one segment, one plant and one vintage of orders.

DCT provides about 90% of the 2027 EBITA step. The Daleville plant makes DCT's chillers and coolant distribution units (CDUs). A SEK 2.1bn order from Q4 2025, priced before the US tariff expansion of April 2026, ships through 2027. The concentration makes the case easy to monitor, because one reported segment margin tests it every quarter. It also makes the case impossible to hedge inside the company, because no second profit engine contributes in 2027.

6

At the fair multiple, the whole return comes from earnings growth.

At 14.77x the model values the shares at SEK 163.73 by March 2028 (+24.6%, 16.7% a year) and SEK 185.75 by September 2029 (+41.3%, 12.6% a year). The forward multiple barely moves, from 14.2x to 14.77x. The gain comes from two-year-forward EPS, which rises about 20% as the 2026 trough rolls out of the forecast window. If consensus proves right, the same 14.77x gives about SEK 185 by March 2028, and a multiple in the high teens becomes defensible (SEK 200 to 230 a share).

7

The timing of entry is the practical question.

Four dated events test the case: the CMD on 11 November 2026; the Q4 2026 report on 28 January 2027, where DCT's growth guidance is likely missed and the real tests are the margin step and the balance of customer advances; the Q1 2027 report, where DCT's margin should be at or above 12.5%; and the Q2 2027 report, where DCT's margin should be at or above 14% with the first year-on-year expansion in gross margin. Precedent says the shares turn one to two quarters before reported gross margin expands year on year, which places the turn between the Q4 2026 and Q2 2027 reports. The cleaner entry point is after the 2027 estimate cuts are through, around the Q1 2027 report. The exception is a CMD that discloses the building blocks of the recovery (capacity, utilisation, localisation share, order-book margin), because those disclosures would let the market model the recovery from its inputs rather than infer it from reported results.

Where we differ from the market. We agree with the sell-side on demand, revenue and the path of the balance sheet, and we agree with the share price on the size of the 2027 earnings cut.

We differ from the sell-side on four numbers. The first is the 2027 group adjusted EBITA margin: 13.3%, against the 14.5% to 15% that consensus implies. The second is cash conversion: 40%, against about 80%. The third is net interest: SEK 440m, against the roughly SEK 300m that the higher brokers imply; only FoodTech sale proceeds could deliver SEK 300m, yet those same brokers keep FoodTech's profit in their forecasts. The fourth is the margin plateau of 2028 to 2029: about 14%, against 15.5% to 16.5%, because rivals' new capacity and warm-water cooling designs begin to bite.

We differ from the share price on five things it fails to credit: the certainty of revenue; covenant headroom (bank definitions exclude leases, so reported leverage of 3.4x is about 2.7x to 2.9x on the covenant basis); FoodTech sale proceeds; a falling tax rate; and overhead leverage that is already visible.

Conclusion. Munters offers a strong, demand-driven earnings step-up at a trough multiple that already prices our 20% cut to consensus. The risk lies in the timing of DCT's margin recovery and in one plant, not in demand. The next six months bring estimate cuts; the following twelve bring the proof.

★Scorecard: the grades for topics 1 to 12

1Operating environment: tailwinds and the absence of headwinds

Key messageThe demand tailwind for Munters is as strong as any in the sector and is already pre-sold through 2027. The headwinds sit squarely on margin and cash; they fade only gradually during 2027, and from 2028 they turn structural, through pricing and the share of chillers in the mix.

Evidence: demand is the strongest in the sector, and peers confirm it is industry-wide. DCT orders more than doubled organically in each of the last three quarters, and group book-to-bill was 2.1x over twelve months (calculated). Hyperscaler capital spending is forecast to rise 82% in 2026. AI rack densities of 40 to over 100 kW double the mechanical and electrical content per megawatt, and the share of AI chips that are liquid-cooled rises from 14% in 2024 to about 60% in 2027. Peers report the same demand: Belimo's data-centre revenue rose 93%, Modine's data-centre sales rose 90% with a USD 4bn framework agreement, and Johnson Controls' backlog stands at USD 21bn. When grid connections slip, customers reallocate orders rather than cancel them, and Munters' custom contracts recover cost plus margin if a customer terminates.

Evidence: every headwind sits on margin and cash, not on demand.

  • Input availability. Pumps, fans, electronics and heat exchangers are scarce; Munters lost SEK 300m of Q2 sales and, because its purchasing scale is modest, is "not always prioritised by suppliers".
  • Metals. Steel is up 32% and copper 18% year to date; there is no evidence of indexation in contracts, and price rises take 12 to 18 months to pass through.
  • Tariffs. US Section 232 tariffs cost 2 points of DCT margin in Q3 2026; the effect is fading.
  • Currency. The SEK is unhedged: a 10% appreciation cuts EBIT by SEK 310m, about 17% of 2025 adjusted EBITA.
  • Interest rates. Munters' debt is at variable rates while rates are rising.
  • AI financing. The funding of the AI build-out is cracking before its demand: spreads on neocloud debt are widening, one colocation customer accounts for 14% to 15% of group sales, and colocation providers place about 57% to 60% of DCT orders.

Inference: the environment is demand-rich, margin-poor and time-limited. Order intake is at or near its cyclical peak, because customers' capacity-securing orders, booked up to 24 months ahead, will not repeat. Revenue, by contrast, is early in its upswing. The margin headwinds are strong now and mostly fade through 2027; the exception is the SEK exchange rate, which may worsen.

From 2028 two later-cycle forces turn against Munters. First, rivals' new capacity normalises pricing: Trane is expanding capacity four-fold and Modine its chiller capacity five-fold, Carrier is building a plant in Texas and Daikin one in Tijuana, and Vertiv's capital spending runs at 4% of sales. Second, warm-water designs shift value away from chillers. With inlet water at 45°C, dry coolers can reject the heat without chillers for 60% to 80% of capacity, and chillers make up 37% of DCT's sales mix and 49% of its trailing orders.

So what for the forecasts. Model 2027 revenue with high confidence. Model 2027 orders below 2026 orders (about SEK 22bn against about SEK 27.5bn) without reading the fall as a failure of demand. Treat the tariff as a 2027 tailwind of about SEK 115m, treat the recovery of price over cost as gradual, and treat the SEK exchange rate as the largest unmodelled swing factor (SEK 1.2 of 2027 EPS for each 10% move). Treat 2028 onwards as a margin plateau, not as a continuation of the 2027 step.

Strongest counter-case. The financing of the AI build-out fails before Munters' backlog ships. A funding break at a colocation provider or a neocloud would defer orders and unwind customer advances while Munters carries debt, a large inventory and a dependence on advance funding. An earlier Viewforth analysis put the probability at 10% to 15% over 18 months, with 2027 EPS 30% to 50% lower. This tail risk is the only one that hits orders, cash and the multiple at once.
What would change our view. Two consecutive quarters of DCT orders below SEK 2.5bn; a hyperscaler or NVIDIA reference design that drops chillers; or USD/SEK below 9.0. On the positive side, evidence that component lead times are shortening would help; they are currently 12 to 16 weeks and lengthening.
Where we differ from the market. We agree with the sell-side on demand. The sell-side presents the tariff as DCT's margin problem; we think input availability, ramp costs and old contract prices now matter more and take longer to fix. No broker includes the SEK exchange rate in its scenarios; we treat it as a first-order variable.

Score: 79, set by the Rater. AI data-centre cooling demand is as strong as any in the Sector and pre-sold through 2027 (DCT orders more than doubling for three quarters, backlog 1.8x sales, liquid-cooling penetration 14% to about 60%, peers confirming), and consensus sales growth sits at the 88th percentile; but it reaches about half of sales, input scarcity, metals, the fading Section 232 tariff and an unhedged SEK take from margins now, and rivals' capacity and warm-water designs turn price and chiller mix against it from 2028. Strong funded demand reaching the value-driving segment but time-limited and margin-trimmed, so above the External change forces group's 70 and just above RELX, below Arteche's broader, longer-dated grid forces.

2Internally-driven corporate change forces and the absence of problems

Key messageMunters' internal change is strong, broad and backed by its main owner, but all of it rests on one fulcrum: the Daleville ramp reaching efficient throughput. The execution record says to add a quarter to every timetable management gives.

Evidence: leadership changed at every level within six weeks. Stefan Aspman became CEO on 14 September 2026, earlier than the October start first announced. As head of DCT from 2022 to 2025 he grew its adjusted EBITA from SEK 84m to SEK 1.15bn and its orders from SEK 6.2bn to SEK 13.9bn; his earlier career at Sandvik centred on value-based pricing. New heads of DCT (Pellegrino) and AirTech (Cook) took over in the same six weeks. End-to-end ownership by business area replaced regional silos, a new enterprise-transformation function took charge of AI and automation, and investor relations joined group management.

Evidence: the main owner backs a portfolio reset. FAM AB, the Wallenberg investment company that owns 28.3%, supports the sale of non-core businesses. FoodTech Equipment was sold in 2025 for EUR 97.5m. The remaining FoodTech business (Speria: SEK 1.75bn of sales at a 17% margin and SEK 354m of annual recurring revenue) is in a sale process run by Evercore, with indicative bids due in late October 2026.

Evidence: self-help and capacity are already in place. AirTech's restructuring (about 200 roles; savings of SEK 250m to 300m a year) had delivered over SEK 100m by mid-2026, ahead of plan, and AirTech's underlying margin rose from 7.0% to 10.4% year on year in Q3. Product platforms are standardised (SyCool Split, Circlemiser). The Daleville expansion is complete: 565,000 square feet, about 600 staff and the full product suite, including Geoclima chillers; management says the site can support SEK 2.5bn to over SEK 3bn of quarterly sales. Capital spending ran at 5% to 7% of sales, and operating working capital is 4.2% of sales against a 10% to 13% target. Insiders have bought shares (the new CEO on 17 July 2026), and no insider has sold in twelve months.

Evidence: the problems are execution slips presented as timing.

  • Management described DCT as "one quarter behind" in each of Q1, Q2 and Q3 2026.
  • Tariff relief was promised for after Q1 2026, then for after Q3 2026, then for "full-year 2027"; management now calls it "optimisation".
  • DCT's margin before tariffs fell while its volume rose.
  • Controls weakened: supplier compliance with the code of conduct fell from 99% to 92%, there is no internal audit function, and employee turnover is 18.6%.
  • The CEO, the divisional heads and the functions all changed at once, in the middle of the ramp, and the new CEO's stated priority is "growth over temporary margin noise".
  • Earnings quality is weak: adjusted EBITA exceeded operating profit by SEK 634m in 2025, and 2026 adjusted figures include a SEK 78m property gain and a cancellation fee worth 2.5 points of margin.
  • The team has no proven operator of large-scale US manufacturing, and none has been hired.

Inference: the direction is right and well funded, but the execution system is the weak link. Customer advances paid for the Daleville build, and FoodTech proceeds can repair the balance sheet, so capital is not the constraint. The constraint is execution: repeated delays of "one quarter" are the classic signature of a problem that lasts longer than first stated. The change of CEO does not bring fresh eyes to the operational problem, because Aspman ran DCT during the ramp that is now behind plan. His first actions are the right kind (direct intervention in the supply chain, qualifying secondary suppliers, customer-approved alternative parts, simplification), but there is no hard evidence of improvement yet.

So what for the forecasts. Internal change supports a strong revenue path, a credible AirTech margin (11.5% in 2027 and 12% in 2028) and a repaired balance sheet. It argues for a DCT margin recovery that comes later and is smaller than consensus expects, and for adding one quarter to any management timetable. The FoodTech sale is positive for risk and optionality but slightly negative for EPS (about -2.5% in 2027 and -4% to -5% from 2028) unless Munters redeploys the proceeds.

Strongest counter-case. The reorganisation and the pricing-led CEO deliver a turnaround like Vertiv's: repriced orders ship, the chiller line reaches proficiency by Q2 2027, and DCT reports a 16% margin by mid-2027. That outcome is our bull case (2027 EPS SEK 9.4), not our base case.
What would change our view. Positively, the hiring of a proven operations leader for DCT, or a CMD that discloses Daleville's capacity and utilisation with a dated DCT margin target. Negatively, a fourth "one quarter behind" at the Q4 2026 report.
Where we differ from the market. The sell-side reads the CEO change and the reorganisation as catalysts for execution (Jefferies: "delayed, not derailed"). We agree on intent but give more weight to the record of slippage, so we add a lag to management's timetable rather than accept it.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. Broad, owner-backed change with parts already working (AirTech restructuring ahead of plan, underlying margin 7.0% to 10.4%; the Daleville build, a large strategic move, in place; FoodTech sale under way; new CEO and divisional heads), but the fulcrum, ramp proficiency at Daleville, is going the wrong way (pre-tariff DCT margin down about 300bp as volume rose 32%, three 'one quarter behind' slips), with earnings-quality gaps and 3.4x leverage. A clear but partly offset positive, a little above the Internal change forces group's 56 because the capacity build and AirTech self-help are large and evidenced, between Odfjell Drilling and ASML.

3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Key messageMunters is a sub-scale, cooling-only challenger in the most favourable phase of a supportive industry, and it captures that phase's volume more than its excess profits. It has a genuine moat only in AirTech, a financial profile that is below average today but strong in potential, and a management team that is excellent commercially but unproven operationally.

Industry structure: Munters is two companies. In industrial desiccant dehumidification (AirTech) it is number one in a global duopoly with Seibu Giken. Customers face high validation and switching costs (months of revalidation; equipment that lasts 10 to 25 years), and the aftermarket provides over 40% of AirTech's sales at high-double-digit margins. Asian rotor makers have eroded the standard battery-manufacturing end of the market, where Munters chose to lose share rather than discount.

In data-centre cooling (DCT), Munters is a fast-growing challenger, roughly fourth to sixth in the market. It has about 8% to 10% of hyperscale cooling against Vertiv's 35% to 45%, and about 3% of a USD 18.8bn thermal-management market growing about 17% a year to 2030 (calculated). The Western majors behave as a disciplined oligopoly: their operating margins are 13% to 19% (Vertiv's 20% to 23%), and list prices rose about 10% in Q3 2026. Chinese and other Asian makers put volume first wherever products standardise.

DCT's position in the value chain is weak on three sides. Buyers are concentrated and powerful: hyperscalers place 36% to 40% of DCT orders, deliberately use several suppliers and seek cooling 30% to 40% cheaper than enterprise builds. Suppliers allocate scarce parts to larger buyers. Integrated rivals (Vertiv, Schneider with Motivair, Eaton with Boyd, Ecolab with CoolIT, and Johnson Controls with 40,000 field staff) capture the system-level value above Munters. Munters' share of data-centre cooling is therefore partly "rented" from today's shortage of capacity, and the share can revert when rivals' capacity lands.

Business model: moats in AirTech, capabilities in DCT. DCT's capabilities are real: energy-efficiency intellectual property (indirect evaporative cooling, the SyCool thermosiphon, pumped-refrigerant patents); custom chilled-water engineering from Geoclima (SEK 400m of sales at acquisition and over SEK 6bn of orders since); relationships with colocation providers; and favourable contract terms (advances of 10% to 30% within 60 to 90 days, and cost plus margin on termination). DCT lacks five things its larger rivals have: procurement scale, an integrated power-and-cooling offer, a place in NVIDIA's reference architectures, its own direct-to-chip cold plates (ZutaCore is a partner), and a North American service network. Munters supplies "the box" in a sector where the evidence says value migrates to the specified component, as the margins of Belimo (EBIT 20.8%) and Carel (EBITDA 22.5%) show.

Financial profile: below average now, above average in potential. The current figures are weak, but incremental returns are very high, because customers fund DCT's growth through advances and capital spending is only about 5% of sales.

Management: excellent commercially, unproven operationally. The ambition is large: SEK 20bn of sales, reached organically and excluding FoodTech, the largest ambition in Viewforth's peer cohort. The tone is honest, and governance is good: one share carries one vote, the board is independent, incentives are cash-settled with mandatory reinvestment in shares, and 80% of the short-term incentive depends on adjusted EBITA growth and 20% on working capital. Communication quantifies some items (tariff points, lost sales, savings) but gives no capacity, utilisation or bridge from price to cost. Capital allocation is good, not outstanding: the Geoclima and MTech acquisitions were excellent, the investment in battery-equipment capacity in AirTech was not, the dividend was paid above the policy range (at 53% of earnings) while leverage rose, and there are no buybacks.

Inference and so what. Munters is a moated industrial franchise attached to an un-moated, very fast-growing data-centre business that now drives the value. The industry structure supports Munters now and becomes fragile beyond about 2027. For the model, high revenue growth is credible; DCT's margin should be modelled below its 2024 to 2025 peaks of 19.5% to 22.8% across the four-year view (our 14.7%, 16.0%, 15.5% and 15.0% for 2027 to 2030); and AirTech's margin recovers structurally.

Strongest counter-case. Jefferies argues that a technology-agnostic portfolio, spanning air to liquid cooling, with facility-scale integration and high switching costs, protects Munters' share through shifts in data-centre architecture. The Q3 2026 chiller data also cut against our view for now: chillers were 49% of orders, and management says chillers and CDUs carry higher margins than air handlers, so chiller demand is strengthening, not weakening.
What would change our view. Munters gaining reference-architecture status with NVIDIA or a hyperscaler; a service franchise emerging in DCT (DCT service is 7% of DCT sales and flat); or evidence of pricing power in DCT's gross margin, which has not yet appeared.
Where we differ from the market. The bulls see a moat in DCT; we see valuable capabilities in an industry structure that rewards scale and integration. DNB Carnegie's structural concern (rivals catching up on capacity, and a limited aftermarket) is close to ours for 2028 onwards.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. A genuine moat only in industrial desiccant dehumidification (duopoly, aftermarket above 40%); the data-centre business that now drives value is a sub-scale, un-moated challenger facing powerful hyperscaler buyers, supplier allocation and integrated rivals, with share partly rented from scarcity; management is commercially strong but operationally unproven. ROIC 5% (37th percentile) and gross margin at a seven-year low understate customer-funded incremental returns, but predictability is low and leverage high, so coherent with the groups (40, 45, 36, 60): one deep moat inside an ordinary whole, between Xvivo and Judges Scientific.

4Guidance conservatism, expectation management and the delivery record

Key messageMunters holds its guidance rather than raising it: the guidance is easy on growth and demanding on margin, and the 2026 DCT growth figure will probably be missed. The sell-side has set 2027 expectations above anything management will commit to, so the set-up favours further estimate cuts before it favours upgrades.

Evidence: formal guidance is sparse, and the one hard 2026 number needs an unlikely fourth quarter. The only quantified 2026 item is DCT sales growth of 30% to 40%, "heavily back-end loaded". Meeting it needs Q4 DCT sales of about SEK 2.7bn organically (SEK 3.1bn or more as reported), against SEK 1,794m in Q3. We model SEK 2,350m and Jefferies SEK 2.5bn, so a miss is probable (70%). The promise of "improving profitability in H2" will be met only modestly (an H2 group margin of 11.7% against 10.9% in H1). Management has also made the high-teens DCT margin goal less time-bound, now speaking of "a clear step" near term and "continued progress next year".

Evidence: the record is one of beats on orders and misses on profit. Orders beat consensus every quarter, but Q4 2025 EBITA came in 23% below consensus, and FY2026 consensus EPS fell 22% over twelve months while FY2027 consensus rose 22%. An earlier Viewforth label for management, "conservative sandbagger", does not fit the last 18 months; "honest tracker with delay creep" does.

Inference: guidance is not conservative where it matters. Growth guidance is easy, the margin ambition is demanding and undated, and the one hard 2026 number will be missed. The sell-side has filled the gap with a 2027 forecast that reaches the mid-term margin target in the first year after the ramp, a level management has carefully declined to endorse. The company is therefore not keeping expectations conservative; the brokers are trimming them after each quarter.

So what for the next two events. Do not expect guidance upgrades during the year; positive surprises will come through reported results. The CMD will most likely hold the group targets (55%), add a high-teens DCT margin ambition with a 2028 horizon, and may formalise SEK 20bn of sales excluding FoodTech for 2028. That target would not be a raise, because consensus already has about SEK 21.8bn. The 2027 outlook at the Q4 report will probably be strong on DCT volume (growth of 40% or more, close to our +47%) and vague on margin, the same shape as the 2026 outlook.

Strongest counter-case. Investor relations now sits in group management, and a new CEO wants to reset credibility; together they could produce a CMD that discloses the building blocks (capacity, utilisation, localisation share, the logic of the order-book margin). Such a CMD would not raise guidance, but it would let the market model the recovery, which is worth more than a target.
What would change our view. A dated DCT margin target for 2027 with the building blocks behind it, or an explicit statement on the 2027 margin in the outlook at the Q4 report.
Where we differ from the market. Consensus treats the 2027 margin recovery as if management had guided to it; we treat the recovery to the margin target as a 2028 event in our base case, consistent with the base rate for ramp recoveries and with the company's own refusal to date it.

Score: 33, set by the Rater. Formal guidance is sparse, easy on growth and demanding on margin (above 14% never achieved for a full year); the record over 18 months is misses on profit (Q4 2025 EBITA 23% below consensus, Q2 2026 miss, Q3 DCT margin 150bp short), tariff relief re-timed four times, three 'one quarter behind' delays, FY2026 consensus cut 22%, and the one quantified 2026 item (DCT growth 30-40%) probably missed. Numbers are honest but timing reliably slips and the company does nothing to keep 2027 consensus conservative, so below the Guidance group's 40, between Fevertree and Solid State.

5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope and feedback loops

Key messageOperating and financial leverage are both high, and both turn from headwind to tailwind in 2027, so 20% revenue growth becomes a 66% EPS step. But the largest single block of that step is gross-margin repair in one segment; DCT's pricing power is real only on newer orders and arrives with a 12- to 18-month lag; and from 2028 the same leverage caps margins and widens the downside.

Operating leverage is high, and it works through two levers that are moving in opposite directions.

The first lever, overheads, works for Munters and is the most predictable part of the earnings bridge. Overheads (the costs between gross profit and adjusted EBITA) were about SEK 693m in Q3 2026 against about SEK 677m a year earlier, up 2% while sales rose 18% (calculated). Full-year overheads of about SEK 2.88bn are 17.2% of 2026 sales; they fall to 15.7% of sales in 2027 and 15.2% in 2028 as they grow 9% and then 6%. That fall is worth 150 to 200 basis points of group margin by 2028.

The second lever, gross margin, currently works against Munters. Gross margin was 27.7% in Q3 2026, because cost of goods sold rose 24% while sales rose 18%. History confirms that Munters' margin moves with price over cost and with mix more than with volume: in 2022 revenue rose 41% and the FactSet EBIT margin fell 240 basis points; in 2024 revenue fell 2.5% and the margin rose 210 basis points.

Three rules of thumb size the leverage. Pure volume drop-through in our model is about 21% to 23%, so each SEK 1bn of extra revenue adds about SEK 230m of EBITA. Each point of gross margin on SEK 20bn of sales is worth SEK 200m, or SEK 0.77 of EPS. And the leverage reverses with the same force: the fixed cost base is the largest ever (depreciation rises from SEK 446m in 2025 to about SEK 620m in 2028), so a 15% shortfall in DCT revenue in 2029 would cut DCT's margin from 15.5% to about 11.5% (calculated).

Pricing power is real in AirTech, nominal and lagging in DCT, and latent for 2027. Industry list prices rose about 10% in Q3 2026, and Vertiv reports price rises ahead of cost rises. Munters' CEO says orders are priced to the expected cost at delivery plus a safety margin, and management reports positive net price in the order book. But three facts temper the claim: DCT's gross margin has not yet shown it, hyperscalers extract 30% to 40% discounts and use several suppliers, and Munters' 2021 price rises took until late 2022, 12 to 18 months, to reach revenue.

The vintage of each order is decisive. The SEK 2.1bn order of Q4 2025 was priced before the US tariff expansion of April 2026 and ships through 2027; the SEK 2.0bn order of April 2026 was priced after it. Our base case has DCT's net price over cost at +0.8 points in 2027, zero in 2028 and -0.5 points a year from 2029 as rivals' capacity lands; the industry's history of sticky pricing in heating, ventilation and air conditioning limits how much is given back.

One asymmetry favours the bull case. Orders booked after April 2026 carry the tariff in their price. If localisation of production then removes the tariff cost, the difference becomes a margin windfall. That windfall is the main route to the bull case, and our base case includes only part of it.

Financial leverage is material and uncomfortable, but has two exits. Net debt is 3.4x EBITDA on the company's definition, which includes leases (FactSet net debt SEK 7,149m), and the debt carries variable rates: each extra point of interest costs SEK 49m, or SEK 0.19 of EPS. This gearing amplifies EPS growth by about 1.35x in 2026 and 1.2x in 2027.

  • Exit one: EBITDA growth. Net debt barely falls in our base case, because dividends, bolt-on acquisitions and new leases absorb free cash flow. EBITDA growth alone takes leverage to about 2.8x at end-2026, 2.1x at end-2027 and 1.8x at end-2028.
  • Exit two: a FoodTech sale. A sale takes leverage below 1x by 2028 and cuts interest by about SEK 215m a year while removing about SEK 320m of EBIT. The sale is EPS-neutral to slightly negative, but it lowers risk.

Items below EBIT turn from a headwind into a tailwind. From 2020 to 2025, EBIT rose 94% but net income only 29%. In 2027, EBIT rises 46% and adjusted net income 66%, because interest stays flat in absolute terms and the tax rate drifts down from 31% to 28%.

Cost-out scope is meaningful, but most of it removes temporary costs. About SEK 335m of savings reaches 2027 adjusted EBITA: about SEK 115m from the tariff, about SEK 120m from ramp efficiency and about SEK 100m from AirTech. The total is worth about 1.7 points of group margin, or SEK 1.3 of EPS, and it is phased about 30% in H1 and 70% in H2. A further SEK 200m to 250m arrives in 2028. Structural levers are not quantified and not modelled: Munters' SEK-denominated costs are 10.6% of costs against 2.9% of revenue, and Project ProCure and the enterprise transformation are under way. They are upside from 2028.

Feedback loops are staggered in time. Three loops reinforce the case through 2027: absorption of fixed costs and learning in the plant (the main driver of the P&L), prices catching up as the backlog ships, and the growing installed base (a slow effect). Three loops balance it from 2027 and 2028: the advance float stops growing (about SEK 1.7bn absorbed over 2027 to 2030 as operating working capital rises from 3.9% to 9.2% of sales), rivals' new capacity normalises supply allocations and prices, and warm-water designs reduce chiller content. One negative loop is latent: delivery delays, which today only cause re-sequencing, become a reason to switch supplier once rivals have spare capacity.

The reinforcing and balancing loops pull in opposite directions in 2027, when adjusted net income rises 66% while free cash flow falls 5%. From 2028 to 2030 the loops are correlated, which widens the range of outcomes.

So what for the forecasts. Revenue growth does produce outsized profit growth in 2027 (revenue +20%, adjusted EBITA +41%, adjusted EPS +66%). But about 40% of the EBITA step is gross-margin repair, which needs execution and pricing rather than leverage. From 2028 the same mechanics cap the group margin near 14% and make the downside as large as the upside.

Strongest counter-case. Vertiv from 2022 to 2024: price escalators and index-linked pricing produced a USD 365m price benefit in one year and took Vertiv's operating margin from about 8% to the high teens in four to six quarters, with incremental margins above 50%. If Munters' orders placed after April 2026 carry similar economics, its 2027 drop-through could reach 35% or more.
What would change our view. Group gross margin above 29% by Q2 2027 (our base case is about 28.5% to 29%); year-on-year expansion in DCT's gross margin; or disclosure of the order-book margin at the CMD.
Where we differ from the market. Jefferies calls Munters' leverage "immense" and models it as a volume effect. We model it as gross profit less overheads and find that volume accounts for about SEK 373m of the SEK 779m EBITA step. Consensus gross margin of 31.5% for 2027 (from three brokers) is the least credible line in the consensus build; we have 29.0%.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. Real operating leverage in the overhead line (overheads +2% on sales +18%, worth 150-200bp by 2028) and a fixed base at its largest ever, plus financial gearing amplifying EPS 1.2-1.35x and about SEK 335m of 2027 cost-out, so 20% revenue growth becomes about 66% EPS growth in 2027; but volume drop-through is only about 21-23%, history shows margin moving with price-cost more than volume (2022: revenue +41%, margin -240bp), DCT pricing power is unproven and lagging, and the leverage is variable-rate and uncomfortable. Above the ordinary mix on the strength of gearing that reverses with equal force, short of a proven both-ways 75.

6Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth and for higher growth and margins than the past

Key messageOur forecasts describe a business about to raise EPS 66% in 2027 and double it by 2028 on pre-sold revenue, with margins settling about 1.5 to 2 points above anything in its history. They still sit 21% below consensus in both years, because we rebuild DCT's margin in blocks and with a lag rather than restore it in one year.

DCT carries the forecasts. DCT's revenue more than doubles from 2026 to 2030, and its margin peaks at 16.0% in 2028 before easing as prices normalise. AirTech's margin rises steadily. FoodTech stays consolidated in the base case, at margins of 16% to 17.5%.

The quarterly path shows where the 2027 profit comes from. We forecast DCT sales of SEK 2,350m at an 11.5% margin in Q4 2026, then SEK 2,380m, 2,480m, 2,580m and 2,680m in the four quarters of 2027, at margins of 12.5%, 14.0%, 15.5% and 16.5%. On that path, about two-thirds of the rise in DCT's quarterly EBITA from Q3 2026 to Q4 2027 comes from the margin recovery and one-third from volume, and 57% of DCT's 2027 EBITA falls in H2 (calculated). Group adjusted EBITA margin follows: 11.2% in Q4 2026; 11.5%, 12.9%, 14.1% and 14.5% in the four quarters of 2027; then 13.5% in Q1 2028.

Scope for double-digit growth: yes, front-loaded and organic. Revenue compounds at about 11.8% a year from 2025 to 2030: 14.2% a year to 2028, then 7% to 9%. Adjusted EPS compounds at about 21% a year, from SEK 4.4 to SEK 11.32. Over 2020 to 2025, by contrast, EPS compounded at only about 10.5% a year, because acquisitions drove revenue while interest and tax absorbed the profit. The 2027 step (+66%) is the core of the case; 2028 (+24%) is the second leg; 2029 and 2030 grow at single digits.

Higher margins than the past: yes, but below consensus. Our group margin plateau of 14.0% to 14.3% from 2028 is above every full year in Munters' record. Only DCT's scale justifies it: six sites, about 90,000 m², with a footprint that can take about 50% more volume. The plateau is below the 15.5% to 16.5% that consensus implies for 2028, because prices normalise from 2029 and the mix stays heavy in chillers. Group gross margin recovers to 29.5%, below the 30% to 33% of 2023 to 2024, because DCT, whose gross margin is lower than service-rich AirTech's, rises from 41% to 50% of sales.

What is reliable and what is not. Revenue is reliable, because it is pre-sold (the 2027 range is SEK 18.5bn to 21.0bn), and so are overhead leverage and the AirTech margin. The repair of DCT's gross margin, by about 300 basis points, is both the largest block and the least reliable of the earnings drivers. Cash is the least reliable line of all (2027 free cash flow ranges from -SEK 0.4bn to +SEK 1.2bn), because the SEK 4.1bn advance float is the swing factor. The model's free cash flow is stated before cash costs of items affecting comparability (SEK 150m in each of 2026 and 2027). A later review corrected the model's working-capital line to remove a false SEK 1.7bn inflow, so the leverage path shown here is the corrected one.

Scenarios for 2027: consensus sits at or above our bull case.

  • Bear case (25%). DCT shipments slip two quarters (DCT sales SEK 8.8bn), DCT's margin is 11.5%, AirTech's 10.5%, and SEK 1bn of advances unwinds. Adjusted EBITA is about SEK 2.07bn (11.2% margin), EPS about SEK 5.1 in 2027 and SEK 6.8 in 2028, and leverage about 3.0x.
  • Bull case (25%). DCT sells SEK 10.9bn at a 17% margin with a windfall from localisation, and AirTech reaches 12%. Adjusted EBITA is about SEK 3.13bn (14.8% margin), and EPS about SEK 9.4 in 2027 and SEK 11.6 in 2028.
  • Probability-weighted. 2027 EPS of about SEK 7.45. Consensus (SEK 9.77 for 2027 and SEK 12.00 for 2028) sits at or above the bull case.

The FoodTech overlay, to switch on if a sale is signed. We assume a close on 30 June 2027 and net proceeds of about SEK 4.3bn. Revenue falls by about SEK 1.0bn in 2027 and by SEK 2.1bn to 2.3bn a year thereafter; EBITDA falls by SEK 190m and then by SEK 380m to 420m; net interest falls by SEK 105m and then SEK 215m. Adjusted EPS falls about 2.5% in 2027 and 4% to 5% from 2028, and leverage falls to 0.8x to 1.0x by end-2028.

Where we differ from the market. About 90% of our 2027 gap to consensus is operating: our EBITDA is SEK 525m lower, because our DCT margin is 14.7% against the 17% to 20% consensus implies, we have AirTech growing 1% against 12%, and our gross margin is 29.0% against 31.5%. The rest is net financial cost (SEK 440m against the roughly SEK 304m implied). Our revenue is 6% below the stale median but within the active brokers' range of SEK 20.9bn to 21.7bn. Our free cash flow is about 60% below consensus, partly because of differences in definition.
What would change our view: three dated tests. Q4 2026: DCT revenue of at least SEK 2.35bn at a margin of at least 11.5%. Q1 2027: DCT margin of at least 12.5% and group gross margin of at least 28.5%. Q2 2027: DCT margin of at least 14%, the first year-on-year gross-margin expansion, and operating working capital of at most 5.5% of sales. Failing either of the first two tests moves us to the bear case; passing the third moves us towards the bull case.

Score: 92, set by the Rater. About 25% sits well inside the A band (15-30%), organic and with the margin plateau of 14.0-14.3% above every full year in the record; placed just above the floor because the growth starts from a trough year and is front-loaded (+66% in 2027, single digits by 2029-30), and the largest block, DCT margin repair, is the least reliable.

7Scope for the forecasts to lead to upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6 to 12 months

Key messageOver the next six months our forecasts point to cuts, not upgrades, to 2027 and 2028 consensus. The cuts will be front-loaded into the CMD and the Q4 2026 report and largely complete by April 2027. The scope for upgrades opens with the Q2 and Q3 2027 reports, from a lower base, if the H2 2027 margin step arrives.

The 2027 consensus median is stale, so it will fall even without new information. The FactSet median for 2027 EPS (SEK 9.77) is Nordea's estimate from before the Q3 report. The seven estimates range from SEK 8.18 (Jefferies, 23 October) to SEK 11.61 (Pareto, 9 October), a spread of 40%. The two brokers who have re-run their models since the Q3 miss on DCT's margin sit at SEK 8.0 to 8.8 (DNB Carnegie raised its estimate 2% to SEK 8.80 on higher sales; Jefferies cut 3% to SEK 7.97), which implies group adjusted EBITA margins of about 13.9%. The four brokers above the median imply margins of 14.5% to 16%. When those four update, the median will drift to about SEK 9.0 to 9.3 on no new information; the CMD and the Q4 report then supply the new information.

Revisions are already net negative: consensus EPS fell 2% over one month and 3% over three months, and target prices fell 7% and 10%. Yet 91% of brokers still rate the shares a Buy, and Viewforth's Master Dashboard scores revision momentum at -1 (rating D). DNB Carnegie has changed its rating six times since February 2025 on margin news, and one more downgrade to Hold from a top-three broker around the Q4 report is likely.

Our probabilities: a cut of more than 10% is the most likely outcome for both years. For FY2027 consensus EPS by the Q1 2027 report, we put a cut of more than 10% at 55%, a hold within ±10% at 35%, and a raise at 10%, with a central outcome of SEK 8.5 to 9.0. For FY2028 by April 2028, we put a cut of more than 10% at 45%, a hold at 40% and a raise at 15%, with a central outcome of SEK 10.5 to 11.0 against our SEK 9.51.

The cuts will show as a falling implied margin, not as a falling top line. Over the last six months consensus sales rose 10% and EBITDA 4% while EPS rose 1%: the pattern of "add volume, trim margin" continues. A margin cut of this kind is a milder signal for the share price than a demand cut. A FoodTech signing would force a further, mainly optical cut (about 2.5% for 2027 and 4% to 5% for 2028) when brokers move FoodTech to discontinued operations; it would also remove the double count in any broker forecast that assumed the sale proceeds without removing FoodTech's earnings.

When the direction of revisions turns. Upgrades need two things that the Q2 2027 report (July) can supply: a DCT margin at or above 14% with year-on-year gross-margin expansion, and orders that keep the 2028 revenue line intact. If both arrive, 2028 consensus, cut by then to SEK 10.5 to 11, will be close to what our base case supports (SEK 9.5, with a bull case of 11.6), and net revisions turn positive from H2 2027. If the margin step arrives a quarter late, as the base rate suggests, the turn moves to the Q3 2027 report in October 2027, still within twelve months. The bulls will cite Vertiv as the template (consensus modelled 30% incremental margins; Vertiv delivered 55% and beat serially), but that outcome needs Daleville to reach Vertiv-like proficiency.

The narrative. Today's sell-side narrative is "delayed, not derailed": brokers name the risks (cash conversion, interest, the SEK, the timing of the margin recovery) but do not put them in their numbers. The narrative that would carry upgrades is "conversion proven", built on the first clean quarter of gross-margin expansion, a utilisation figure for Daleville and leverage below 2x. The CMD can start that narrative by disclosing the building blocks, but it cannot finish it.

Guidance. The most likely outcome at the next two events is guidance held and re-timed. A raised outlook is plausible only from the Q3 2027 report, and only if DCT margins are at or above 15% and orders hold. A 2028 outlook of DCT growth in the low-to-mid teens (we have +14%) will read as deceleration against 2027's +47% even if it is on plan, which makes that outlook the event most likely to produce a "reduce" headline in early 2028.

Strongest counter-case. The share price already discounts the cuts, so cuts that arrive without a further operational miss could meet a rising share price. Precedent supports this: shares re-rate one to two quarters before reported gross margin turns, and the sell-side lags the turn by one to two quarters. When the upgrade cycle comes, it will start from a cut estimate base and a trough multiple. That combination is the positively skewed moment, and it sits in mid-2027, not now.
What would change our view. A CMD that dates high-teens DCT margins for 2027, with building blocks behind the target, would be bullish. A CMD that moves the target to 2028 without explanation would confirm our base case but damage the narrative.
Where we differ from the market. The sell-side expects 2027 to turn out as modelled. We expect 2027 consensus to be cut 10% to 15% by April 2027 and revisions to turn between July and October 2027.

Score: 24, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely held and re-timed at the CMD and Q4 report, with the 2026 DCT growth figure probably missed; FY2027 consensus is stale (median from pre-Q3 brokers, updated brokers at SEK 8.0-8.8 against 9.77) and 55% likely cut by more than 10%, about -0.5 to -0.75 of the 20% revenue growth rate, with revisions already negative (3-month EPS -4%, 19th percentile). The only offset is a possible turn from the Q2-Q3 2027 reports on a cut base and a narrative already priced harsher than consensus, so in line with the fourth-set group's 26, between Indutrade and Prosus.

8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, share price, and peers

Key messageMomentum in guidance, estimates, narrative and share price is uniformly negative and specific to Munters, while data-centre peers enjoy premium multiples and upgrades. That configuration typically precedes the best entry points in ramp recoveries, provided the ramp does recover.

Evidence: every momentum reading is negative.

Technical momentumFprice 24% below the 200-day average of SEK 172.8 (50-day SEK 145.8); relative strength at the 10th percentile
Share-price return-33.0%over six months; -20.7% over three; +6.9% over twelve; 52-week range SEK 121 to 212
Sell-side momentumDrevision score -1; EPS -2% over one month; targets -10% over three; 91% Buy, unchanged
Guidance momentumnoneguidance held, with a 2026 DCT growth miss ahead
Narrative momentummixednegative on execution, positive on demand; Q3 read as "exceptional orders, margins lag"

Evidence: the share price has decoupled from its sector, for company-specific reasons. The building-technology basket explains only 25% of Munters' six-month share-price variance (beta 1.08, correlation 0.50). Over six months Munters returned -31% against +10.5% for the basket, and the whole gap of about 40 points is specific to the company: the collapse in DCT's margin, the expansion of Section 232 tariffs, the Q2 miss and the third "one quarter behind". Munters moves most closely with the data-centre cooling names (correlations of 0.58 with Belimo, 0.51 with Zehnder, 0.44 with Carel and 0.39 with LU-VE). The basket excludes the US AI-infrastructure factor (Vertiv, Modine, AAON), which explains part of the apparently company-specific residual: Munters fell 21% over three months while Modine and AAON fell 32% and Vertiv 20%.

Peers: the industry has not been de-rated; Munters has. The data-centre-exposed peers carry sector premiums and positive revisions. LU-VE, for example, trades at 17.5x, the 90th percentile of its own history, after a 61% return over twelve months. Munters trades at 11.3x, the 10th percentile of its ten-year history, with negative revisions.

Inference: the price now moves on Munters' own news, which cuts both ways. Every momentum reading is negative today, and the stock is in the part of its cycle where its price moves on company news, not sector news. On the positive side, the catalysts for a re-rating are internal and dated (the CMD and the Q4, Q1 and Q2 reports), so the path is testable. On the negative side, the sector offers no cushion, and the AI-infrastructure factor (credit conditions, hyperscalers' capital-spending guidance, NVIDIA design news) can hit the share price whatever the quarter shows.

So what for entry timing. Momentum is against the case now and will stay against it through the estimate-cut window; it turns with the first clean gross-margin quarter. For a momentum-aware investor, the signal to act is the Q1 2027 report (DCT margin above 12.5%, gross margin above 28.5%), or an earlier CMD that discloses the building blocks.

Strongest counter-case. A multiple at the 2nd percentile of five years, a share price 24% below its 200-day average and relative strength at the 10th percentile are together the classic set-up for a sharp rebound on any positive surprise. And three insider purchases with no insider sales say that the people closest to the ramp think the share price is wrong.
What would change our view. The share price reclaiming its 50-day average while the active brokers revise upwards; or, negatively, a disappointment from Vertiv or Modine in February 2027 that drags the AI-infrastructure factor down regardless of Munters' own results.
Where we differ from the market. We read the momentum indicators as the market does. We add one point: Munters has fully decoupled from its peers, so peers' strength will not transfer to Munters until its own numbers turn.

Score: 26, set by the Rater. Both measures negative but the sell-side score not in the bottom fifth gives D; every part confirms rather than contradicts (guidance held with a miss ahead, EPS -4% over three months, targets -10%, narrative negative on execution, price 24% below a falling 200-day average and -33% over six months), and peers' strength does not transfer to a company-specific de-rating, so placed at the floor of D.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Key messageThe case is simple in structure but concentrated on one segment's margin and one plant's proficiency. Its 18-month range is wide (2027 EPS of SEK 5.1 to 9.4), modestly skewed down on earnings and clearly down on cash. The case is trackable each quarter but not forecastable from what Munters discloses, and it is exposed to sudden external shocks that can move the share price 20% whatever the quarter shows.

Simplicity: the case is simple to state and concentrated to the point of fragility. DCT provides about 90% of the 2027 EBITA step, and the drivers concentrate on every axis: one plant, two orders, one customer group and one currency. A concentrated case is an advantage for monitoring and a disadvantage for forecasting. One reported segment margin tests the whole forecast each quarter, and nothing offsets a miss on that margin.

The five judgements that move the shares most over one to two years. The base case for 2027 is revenue of SEK 20,050m, DCT sales of SEK 10,120m at a 14.7% margin (DCT EBITA SEK 1,487m), group adjusted EBITA of SEK 2,673m, a 29.5% tax rate and 182.5m shares, giving adjusted EPS of SEK 7.60. Each EPS effect below equals the EBITA change × (1 - 0.295) / 182.5 (calculated).

Two further swing factors are smaller for EPS but matter for the multiple. The FoodTech sale lowers EPS by 2.5% in 2027 and by 4% to 5% from 2028, but takes leverage below 1x and brings in about SEK 24 a share of proceeds. A one-point rise in interest rates lowers EPS by SEK 0.19.

The range of outcomes is wide and skewed down on earnings and cash. 2027 adjusted EPS ranges from SEK 5.1 to 9.4 (-33% to +24%) around our base of SEK 7.60, with a probability-weighted value of about SEK 7.45. 2027 revenue ranges from -8% to +5% around the base, and 2027 free cash flow from -SEK 0.4bn to +SEK 1.2bn. The skew is modestly down on earnings, because the bear case needs only a continuation of 2026's pattern while the bull case needs a pattern Munters has not shown. The skew is clearly down on cash and modestly up on revenue. The 2027 range halves by July 2027; the 2028 range (EPS of SEK 6.8 to 11.6) then becomes the live one, and it is wider because it adds price normalisation and the risk of design changes.

The case is trackable but not forecastable. The four decisive numbers are reported every quarter: DCT orders, DCT sales, DCT margin with the tariff effect, and operating working capital with advances on the balance sheet. The case can therefore be tracked about one quarter after the fact. The mechanism behind those numbers (utilisation, order-book margin, import share, backlog phasing) is not disclosed, so the case cannot be forecast from its inputs. Management's timetables deserve a one-quarter discount; its numbers are reliable.

The sudden risks are external, and any one of them can move the share price 20% whatever the quarter shows.

  • AI financing. CoreWeave's bond yields are near 15%, 74 US data-centre projects are blocked or delayed, and 61 GW of capacity is stranded.
  • Design. An NVIDIA design announcement that works against chillers.
  • Trade. A US trade action on components.
  • Field quality. A quality failure in liquid cooling (probability 5% to 10%; cost SEK 100m to 300m).
  • Currency. SEK appreciation of 15% (probability 10%).

Precedents: contractions last three to six quarters, and the shares turn before the margin does. Munters' own margin swings exceed 400 basis points from peak to trough, with a ten-year standard deviation above 250 basis points against about 150 for peers. In the data-centre crisis of 2017 to 2019, Munters' margin fell from 12.9% to 10.2%, its share price from SEK 69.5 to 32.2 (-54%) and its two-year-forward P/E to 10.7x; FAM replaced the chair and the CEO, and recovery took two years. Peers show the same pattern. Vertiv's operating margin fell to 8% in 2022 and its forward P/E troughed at 11x before reaching 33x by early 2025. Carel's revenue fell 11% and its EBITDA 24% in 2024. At AAON in 2026, overhead costs at the Memphis plant cut gross margin from 28.9% to 24.3%. Ramps run late everywhere (Systemair's Menerga, LU-VE's Texas plant, Modine's design slip): the next stated timetable is usually missed by one to two quarters, and then the recovery arrives.

Strongest counter-case. The case is simpler than it looks. Revenue is pre-sold, three-quarters of the profit step is mechanical, the balance sheet has covenant headroom and a SEK 4bn business to sell, and the only real variable is the quarter in which one plant reaches proficiency.
What would change our view. The dated tests in section 6; any one of the sudden external risks; or a CMD that discloses the mechanism behind the numbers, which would make the case forecastable as well as trackable and lower its riskiness by a grade.
Where we differ from the market. The sell-side knows these risks but has put none of the cash, interest or SEK items into its numbers. The share price has priced them.

Score: 27, set by the Rater. The memo's 2027 EPS cone is SEK 5.1 to 9.4 around 7.60 (-33% to +24%), skewed down on earnings and clearly on cash, and rests on one segment margin from one plant, two order vintages, a colocation customer at 14-15% of sales and an unhedged USD, on 3.4x variable-rate leverage, with sudden external tails (AI financing, chiller design, trade, SEK) that can move the price 20%. Pre-sold revenue, quarterly trackability and a trough multiple keep it off the bottom, so consistent with the Risks groups (38, 36) but lower for the leverage-amplified correlated tail, between Storskogen and Fugro.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Key messageMunters is in late Stalling. The fundamentals of Bottoming are already in place (revenue has turned, the margin trough is plausibly reached, leverage is past its peak), but the estimate cuts are not yet complete. The stock moves to Turning up only with the first clean gross-margin quarter, most likely between April and October 2027.

Evidence. Viewforth's Master Dashboard rule places the starting phase at Stalling. The readings behind it:

  • The two-year-forward multiple sits at the 2nd percentile of five years and the 10th percentile of ten years.
  • Technical momentum is F and sell-side momentum D.
  • FY2026 consensus EPS was cut 22% in twelve months, but FY2027 and FY2028 consensus have not been cut at all, and 91% of brokers rate the shares a Buy.
  • The shares are 33% below their April 2026 high, when the two-year-forward P/E was 19.0x.
  • The business is at a margin trough (DCT 9.7% in Q3 2026, plausibly the trough quarter or one quarter before it), while revenue has turned up decisively (+17.8% in Q3 after -8%, -4% and +6%).

Inference: the stock has stalled on execution, not on demand. It has fallen to the valuation of a collapsing story while the fundamentals of a bottoming story are in place: a visible revenue upturn, a margin trough plausibly reached, a balance sheet past its peak leverage, and a long-horizon owner. Two things are missing for Bottoming: the completion of estimate cuts to 2027 and 2028, and a fall in the share of Buy ratings (the "cleared" set-up in Viewforth's framework). One thing is missing for Turning up: the first clean quarter of year-on-year gross-margin expansion, which our base case places in Q2 to Q3 2027.

The phases therefore run in sequence: late Stalling now; Bottoming between the Q4 2026 report (January 2027) and the Q1 2027 report (April 2027) as the cuts complete; Turning up from the Q2 and Q3 2027 reports if DCT's margin passes 14% and gross margin expands; and Thesis broadening in 2028 if leverage falls below 2x, FoodTech proceeds arrive and a service or liquid-cooling business emerges. The collapsing branch is the 25% bear case.

So what for entry. The phase determines the fair multiple (section 11) and the timing of entry. A Stalling stock whose estimates are still to be cut is best bought in stages: a first position at the CMD if management discloses the building blocks, and the balance after the Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 reports, when the cuts are through and the gross-margin test is set.

Strongest counter-case. The dashboard rule and the share price both say Stalling, but the AI-financing tail and the shift to warm-water designs say the stall could become a collapse in 2028 even if 2027 delivers. The market has not yet priced the reversal of the capacity-scarcity loop for 2029.
What would change our view. Two consecutive quarters of DCT margin above 14% would move the phase to Turning up; two consecutive quarters of DCT orders below SEK 2.5bn would move it towards Collapsing.
Where we differ from the market. The sell-side's language ("delayed, not derailed", "compelling entry point") describes a stock that is Bottoming or Turning up; the share price describes a Stalling one. We side with the share price on timing and with the sell-side on direction.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. The computed Stalling is right for the price and estimates (momentum F/D, FY2027-28 consensus still to be cut by 10-15%, 91% Buy), but the fundamentals of Bottoming are forming (revenue turned to +17.8%, DCT margin plausibly at its trough, leverage past its peak), with Turning up not before the Q2-Q3 2027 reports. Late Stalling, more attractive than a stall with no turn in sight and less than a confirmed Bottoming, between Hellenic Telecom and Storskogen.

11The fair multiple

Key messageThe guideline multiple of 14.77x is the fair multiple for a Stalling stock whose de-rating is its own. The shares already trade at about 14.2x our earnings, so the multiple adds almost nothing to the return. That is the correct reading of a case whose upside comes from earnings delivery, not from a re-rating.

Viewforth's guideline. For the Stalling phase, the guideline fair multiple is 14.77x two-year-forward earnings, the 40th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history. The other reference points in that history are the 10th percentile at 11.2x ("crash"), the 35th at 14.3x ("conservative"), the median at 15.8x ("prudent"), the 75th at 18.9x ("defendable") and the 90th at 22.2x ("mania"). On consensus EPS (SEK 11.67 two years forward) the multiple is now 11.35x, 30% below the guideline; on our EPS it is about 14.2x, within 4% of the guideline.

Our view: 14.77x is the right fair multiple for the next 18 months, for three reasons.

  1. It applies to conservative earnings. We apply the multiple to our EPS, which already sits 21% below consensus, and a 40th-percentile multiple on a conservative earnings base is not a generous valuation.
  2. The stock's own history is the right reference. The de-rating is specific to Munters (section 8: about 75% of the six-month share-price variance is company-specific, and peers trade at premiums), so the stock's own history, not the peer range of 17x to 29x, is the right benchmark. That ten-year history includes the 2017 to 2019 crisis (a 10.7x trough) and the 2024 mania (24x), so its 40th percentile fairly describes a stock that has stalled but not broken.
  3. The fair multiple rises as the phase changes. If the Q2 and Q3 2027 tests are passed and the stock is Turning up, the prudent median of 15.8x becomes appropriate. If 2028 delivers and the thesis broadens (leverage below 1x, a service business), the defendable band of 18.9x is reachable, as it was in 2023 to 2024 and as the re-ratings of Vertiv and Modine show. If the bear case plays out, the crash band of 11.2x applies to a lower EPS.

Cross-checks support a value of about SEK 163 a share (calculated). Enterprise value of about SEK 29bn (FactSet) is about 11x our 2027 adjusted EBITA of SEK 2,673m and about 9.4x the SEK 3.09bn that consensus implies. A sum of the parts on our 2027 numbers, at DNB Carnegie's segment multiples, also gives about SEK 163 a share, the same as the model's 18-month value. Today's share price equals Jefferies' downside case (SEK 130, which assumes a 10% long-term EBIT margin and 14x 2027 EV/EBIT). Strategic buyers have paid premia for data-centre thermal assets (Eaton for Boyd, USD 9.5bn; Ecolab for CoolIT, USD 4.75bn); on the Analyst's reading, those premia put a floor of 40% to 60% under the equity while it trades at trough multiples.

Strongest counter-case. DNB Carnegie warns that if hyperscaler sales growth disappoints, Munters' multiple will revert to that of small-cap capital-goods companies (about 11x to 13x). The stock would then deserve the crash band rather than the 40th percentile, and a multiple of 14.77x would overstate its value by 25%. A trailing P/E of about 25x on 2025 adjusted EPS of SEK 5.28 is also a reminder that the share price already pays for part of the recovery.
What would change our view. Passing the Q2 2027 test would justify 15.8x; failing the Q1 2027 test would justify 11.2x on bear-case EPS.
Where we differ from the market. The sell-side's targets (median SEK 200; Jefferies and DNB Carnegie SEK 190; Pareto and UBS SEK 240 to 245) apply 15x to 17x EV/EBIT to consensus earnings. We apply a similar multiple to lower earnings, which is why our 18-month value is SEK 164, not SEK 200.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. Raw readings are cheap on both (A), but part of the cheapness is a stale consensus: on the memo's EPS, 21% lower, the two-year-forward P/E is about 14.2x, around the 37th percentile of its own history (neutral) and still about a quarter cheaper than normal against peers, and a Stalling stock deserves a below-median multiple; I move the letter to B and place it in the lower half of the band.

12Total shareholder return via the Dupont framework

Key messageAt the guideline fair multiple, the shares return about 25% over 18 months and about 41% over three years, almost entirely from earnings growth as the 2026 trough rolls out of the forward window. On a forward basis the multiple contributes almost nothing and dividends add 3 to 5 points. The return is therefore a bet on the delivery of a 2027 to 2028 earnings step that the share price already discounts at a fifth below consensus.

The model's return at the guideline fair multiple of 14.77x, from a share price of SEK 131.45.

The negative "multiple" line reflects the 2026 trough, not a de-rating. The template splits the return on a trailing basis (calculated). Its "earnings" line is the growth in trailing adjusted EPS from SEK 5.28 in 2025 (Viewforth's definition) to about SEK 8.3 at March 2028 (+57%) and about SEK 10.3 at September 2029 (+96%). Its "multiple" line is the fall in the trailing P/E from about 25x today (SEK 131.45 divided by 5.28) to about 19.7x and 18x respectively. The negative multiple line therefore does not mean the stock de-rates. It means the share price already pays for part of the recovery, because 2026 is a trough year.

On a two-year-forward basis, the same 18-month return breaks down into three parts. Earnings contribute about +20%, as two-year-forward EPS rises from about SEK 9.3 today (a blend of 2027 and 2028) to about SEK 11.1 at March 2028 (a blend of 2029 and 2030). The multiple contributes about +4%, from 14.2x to 14.77x. Dividends contribute +3% (SEK 1.60 plus SEK 2.30). On either basis the conclusion is the same: the return comes from earnings, and those earnings are the 2027 to 2028 step.

What drives the return, in order of size.

  1. DCT's conversion of the backlog into revenue (DCT sales rising from SEK 6.9bn to SEK 11.5bn over 2026 to 2028) provides about half of the EBITA growth.
  2. DCT's margin repair from 11.6% to 16.0% (tariff, ramp, price over cost) provides about 40%.
  3. AirTech at an 11.5% to 12% margin, plus overhead leverage, provides about 10%.
  4. Tailwinds below EBIT (interest flat in absolute terms while profit doubles; tax falling from 31% to 28%) turn EBITA growth of 41% in 2027 into EPS growth of 66%.
  5. Dividends rise to SEK 3.20 for 2028 (35% to 41% of reported EPS).

Three things are not in the return: a FoodTech sale (EPS-neutral to -5%, but positive for the multiple through lower leverage), buybacks (none are planned), and any re-rating beyond the guideline multiple.

The range of returns to March 2028 (calculated; dividends included).

  • Bear case (25%). 2028 EPS of about SEK 6.8 at the crash band of 11.2x gives about SEK 76 to 85 a share, a return of -35% to -40%.
  • Base case (50%). SEK 164 a share, a return of +25%.
  • Bull case (25%). 2028 EPS of SEK 11.6 and 2029 EPS of about SEK 13, at the prudent-to-defendable bands of 15.8x to 18.9x, give about SEK 200 to 235 a share, a return of +50% to +80%.
  • Probability-weighted. About SEK 156 to 160 a share, a return of about +20% including dividends.
  • Consensus. If consensus EPS (SEK 12.00 for 2028 and 12.80 for 2029) is right, 14.77x alone gives about SEK 185 by March 2028 (+41%).

Each turn of the multiple is worth about SEK 11 a share, or 8%.

Over three years, the return carries extra risks and extra upside. The three-year column (SEK 185.75, +41%, 12.6% a year) adds EPS growth of 24% in 2028 and 12% in 2029 at the same multiple. It also carries three risks that the 18-month return does not: price normalisation from 2029, the shift to warm-water designs that need fewer chillers, and the dilution from a FoodTech exit. Against those, it carries the upside of the phase moving to Turning up or Thesis broadening, when the multiple, not just earnings, does the work.

Strongest counter-case. The split shows the stock already at 25x trailing earnings. If 2027 falls to the bear case, the trailing multiple normalises on earnings that never arrive, and the -22.6% "multiple" line becomes a real loss rather than an accounting artefact. The return is only as good as DCT's margins in Q1 to Q3 2027.
What would change our view. The dated tests, or a FoodTech sale with the proceeds returned to shareholders, which would add about 1% to EPS through buybacks (on an earlier Viewforth calculation) and more to the multiple.
Where we differ from the market. The sell-side's targets of SEK 190 to 245 equal our bull case, or consensus EPS at the fair multiple; our base case is SEK 164 in 18 months. The difference lies entirely in the level of 2027 to 2028 earnings, not in the multiple.

Score: 73, set by the Rater. About +19-20% sits at the B/C boundary, about 74-75 on the scale; the three-year check (+41%, 12.6% a year) is supportive and the return is all earnings, but the fat, correlated lower tail (25% at -35% to -40%) moves it to the top of C.

13Summary conclusion

Munters is a strong, demand-driven earnings step-up, bought at a multiple that already assumes the sell-side is wrong by a fifth. Demand is pre-sold through 2027, three-quarters of the 2027 profit step is mechanical, the balance sheet is past its peak leverage with a SEK 4bn business to sell, and a long-horizon owner has shown it will act if the ramp fails.

One uncertain quarter of the profit step carries the whole share-price case. That quarter is DCT's margin on each unit shipped from one plant in Virginia, and the record says it arrives late: in H2 2027 in our base case, a quarter later than management implies, and in 2028 for the margin target that consensus places in 2027.

The next six months bring cuts; the following twelve bring the proof. 2027 estimates will be cut 10% to 15%, into a share price that has already fallen 33% while peers rose. The dated proof follows: a DCT margin above 12.5% in Q1 2027, then above 14% in Q2 2027 with gross margin expanding year on year.

The return is attractive, and it comes from earnings. At the guideline 14.77x, the base-case return is about +25% to March 2028 and +41% to September 2029, all from earnings. The bull case returns +50% to +80% and the bear case -35% to -40%; the probability-weighted return is about +20%.

The practical implication: stage the entry. The case is attractive on a 12- to 24-month view, but the skew becomes unusually positive only once the estimate cuts are through and the gross-margin turn is visible. The CMD on 11 November is the first chance to see whether management will disclose the building blocks (Daleville's capacity and utilisation, the localisation share, the order-book margin, the use of FoodTech proceeds) that would let the market model the recovery rather than wait for it. A first tranche on a CMD that discloses those building blocks, and the balance after the Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 reports, fits the shape of the risk.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength78

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 78, set by the Rater. Top-tier, funded external demand (topic 1, 79) already pre-sold into revenue turns into forecast EPS growth of about 25% a year and a doubling by 2028 (topic 6, A), with three-quarters of the 2027 profit step on demonstrated or mechanical ground; but the internal conversion (topic 2, 60) is the weak link, the step is not yet visible in results (margins still falling) and it plateaus from 2028, so below Arteche's 80.

Foundations' Robustness40

Foundations' Robustness: 40, set by the Rater. A durable AirTech moat and a customer-funded growth model are outweighed by a sub-scale, un-moated position in the data-centre business that now carries the value, low and unpredictable margins, 3.4x leverage and unclean earnings (topic 3, 46), while the delivery record of repeated timing slips and profit misses (topic 4, 33) adds no robustness.

Setups' Fit/Crispness64

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 64, set by the Rater. In substance the case is a Demand-driven EPS Upgrader with the demand step-up and the capacity in place (backlog 1.8x sales, Daleville built), but the delivery element is the current problem (DCT margin halved, ramp behind plan), which blurs the fit and leaves it straddling a Major CfC Clearing that has not yet cleared; estimates not yet cut and the price are left to topics 7 and 12.

Case Riskiness25

Case Riskiness: 25, set by the Rater. A simple story with a wide, down-skewed cone (topic 9, 27) concentrated on one plant's margin, geared at 3.4x on variable-rate debt and exposed to AI-trade sentiment and financing shocks that can hit orders, cash and the multiple together; quarterly trackability and a trough multiple are the only cushions.

Glossary

AirTech: Munters' industrial air-treatment and dehumidification division.

Book-to-bill: orders received divided by sales.

CDU: coolant distribution unit, which circulates liquid coolant to the servers.

CMD: Capital Markets Day, 11 November 2026.

Colocation provider: a company that leases data-centre space and power to several tenants.

DCT: Data Center Technologies, Munters' data-centre cooling division.

Drop-through: the share of extra revenue that becomes extra EBITA.

EV/EBIT: enterprise value divided by EBIT.

FAM: FAM AB, the Wallenberg investment company that owns 28.3% of Munters.

Hyperscaler: one of the largest cloud operators that build their own data centres.

Neocloud: a newer, specialist provider of AI computing capacity, often debt-funded.

Operating working capital: the company's measure of working capital, net of customer advances.

ROIC: return on invested capital.

Section 232: US tariffs on imported steel, aluminium and derived products.

Two-year-forward P/E: share price divided by a blend of the next two financial years' EPS.

Warm-water design: liquid cooling that runs at high water temperatures, so heat can be rejected by dry coolers without chillers.
